textbookText: Class: 4 Holothuroidea (Gr; holothurion- sea cucumber; eidos-form) i. They are commonly called sea cucumber. ii. Body is elongated in oral- aboral axis having mouth at the one end and anus at the other end. iii. Mouth is surrounded by tentacles. iv. Tube feet are present for locomotion cloaca contains respiratory tree. v. Larvae are called auricularia and doliolaria.
Example: Holothuria (sea cucumber), Cucumaria (sea cucumber)
Sub-phylum: Pelmatozoa (Gr; pelmatos-stalk; zoon-animal): They are stalked and there is only one class.

Class: 5 Crinoidea i. They are commonly called sea lilies or feather star. ii. Body is attached to substratum by an aboral stalk most of the time. But feather star is free swimming. iii. Mouth and anus on the oral surface. iv. Pedicellaria, spines and madreporite are absent and tube feet without suckers. v. Larva is called doliolaria.
Example: Antedon (feather star), sea lilies etc.

Project work Collect different type of small invertebrates found in your locality (take precautions at the time of collection). Classify them into different phylum according to their external features. Now, prepare a report or power point presentation and present in the class. 8.2.10 PHYLUM: CHORDATA (Gr; chorde-string or cord; ata-bearing)

Phylum Chordata is the last major group of kingdom animalia which was created by Balfour in 1880. The term ‘chordata’ is derived from two Greek words ‘chorde’ means string or cord and ‘ata’ means bearing. It indicates that these animals have a common characteristic which is a stiff supporting rod like structure on the back called notochord. (Gr; noton-back; L; chordacord). Notochord is found in all the member of this phylum at some stage of their life. Following are the major characters of phylum chordata:

1. Presence of notochord: An elongated, flexible and supporting rod like structure present in mid dorsal line from head to tail. It lies beneath the nerve cord and above the alimentary canal. It persists throughout the life in lower chordates (protochordates) but embryonic notochord is replaced by vertebral column in the adult of higher chordates (vertebrates)

2. Dorsal tubular nerve cord: A longitudinal hollow nerve cord of ectodermal origin extends lengthwise of the body above notochord. In vertebrates, its anterior region form brain which is protected by cranium and posterior part form spinal cord which is protected by vertebral column.

3. Presence of pharyngeal gill slits: Series of paired gill slits present on the lateral wall of pharynx at some stages of development in all chordates. In primitive chordates and lower aquatic vertebrates, gill slits or gill clefts remain throughout the life for breathing but disappear in the adult of higher vertebrates.
Figure 8.2.18 A chordate’s body plan Other general characters:

4. They are aquatic, terrestrial and aerial. Mostly free living and very few are parasitic. 5. They are triploblastic, metamerically segmented and bilaterally symmetrical. 6. They have schizocoel or true coelom formed by splitting of mesoderm in the embryonic

stage. Enterocoelom is found in proto chordates. 7. Exoskeleton is often present and well developed and endoskeleton is cartilaginous or bony in majority of them 8. There is complete alimentary canal with digestive glands. 9. Circulatory system is closed type, consists of ventrally located heart and all types of blood vessels. 10. Some of them have post anal tail beyond anus. 11. Respiratory system is well developed consisting of gills or lung or moist skin. 12. They have kidneys for excretion. 13. They have well developed nervous system 14. Majority of them have well developed sensory organs such as eye, auditory organ, olfactory organs, taste receptors etc. 15. Sexes are separate. Mostly direct development and some of them have indirect development.

Figure 8.2.19 classification of chordata Phylum Chordata consists of four sub-phyla which are Hemichordata, Urochordata, Cephalochordata and Vertebrata. First three sub-phyla are primitive chordates which are exclusively marine, relatively small and without vertebral column and also called protochordates. They also lack cranium and hence placed in group acraniata. Last sub-phylum vertebrata consist of animals which are more advanced and specific over these protochorates and hence called Euchordates. Their notochord is replaced by vertebral column in adult and have cranium and hence placed in the group craniata.
1. Hemichordata (Gr; hemi-half; chorde-cord): i. They are exclusively marine, solitary or colonial and mostly tubicolous (living inside

self-constructed tube). ii. Body is soft and worm like. iii. Notochord is present at the anterior region of the body. iv. Their body is divided into three regions- proboscis, collar and trunk Examples: Balanoglossus(tongue worm or acorn worm), Saccoglossus etc.

2. Urochordata (Gr;oura-a tail; chorde-cord) or Tunicata i. They are also exclusively marine found at all depth and commonly called as “tunicates” ii. Notochord and nerve cord are present only in larva but absent in adults. iii. They show retrogressive metamorphosis as the larval form is more advanced than adult. iv. Adult body is mostly sedentary, enclosed within leathery test or tunic.
Example: Herdmania (sea squirt), Ascidia etc.
